text: In principle, yes. [[asteroid|Asteroids]] are leftover building blocks of the [[solar-system|solar system]], and many contain useful materials. Some are rich in iron and nickel, with small amounts of precious metals like platinum. Others hold water locked in clay minerals or as ice.

Space agencies have already visited asteroids and brought back samples. Japan's Hayabusa2 returned about 5 grams from asteroid Ryugu in 2020. NASA's OSIRIS-REx brought back about 120 grams from asteroid Bennu in 2023. But those missions cost hundreds of millions of dollars to collect a few spoonfuls.
Turning that into real mining would need cheaper rockets, robots that work on their own and a way to make money from what they dig. Nobody has done it yet.

st.prompt: If a company brought a huge platinum-rich asteroid back to Earth, what would most likely happen to the price of platinum?

options.t: It would fall sharply, because platinum would no longer be rare
It would rise, because space platinum is special
It would stay exactly the same

st.reveal: Things are expensive partly because they are scarce. Flooding the market with platinum would make it cheaper. That is one reason many experts think space miners would sell their materials in space rather than on Earth.

sec.t:
Most asteroids [[orbit|orbit]] the Sun between Mars and Jupiter, in the [[asteroidbelt|asteroid belt]]. Some, called near-Earth asteroids, come closer to us and are easier to reach.

Asteroids come in different types. Dark, carbon-rich ones like Ryugu and Bennu hold water and the chemicals of life. Stony ones are like the rocks of Earth's crust. A few are mostly metal. The best-known metal-rich asteroid is 16 Psyche, about 280 km across at its widest. NASA launched a spacecraft called Psyche in October 2023 to study it. It should arrive in 2029.

Many [[@meteorites|meteorites]] that fall on Earth are broken bits of asteroids, which is how scientists first learned what asteroids are made of.

Mining in [[@gravity-planets|near-zero gravity]] is strange. A small asteroid's [[gravity|gravity]] is so weak that a robot could bounce off with one hard push. When OSIRIS-REx touched Bennu in 2020, its sampling arm sank in as if the surface were a ball pit. The asteroid turned out to be a loose pile of rubble, not solid rock.

Ideas for future mining include wrapping a small asteroid in a bag, heating rocks to drive water out as steam, or using magnets to collect metal grains. Cheaper [[@reusable-rockets|reusable rockets]] make these plans seem less far-fetched than they did 20 years ago, but none has been tested on a real asteroid.

In the 2010s, two American start-ups promised to mine asteroids. Both ran short of money and were taken over by other companies before they ever launched a mining mission.

The Outer Space Treaty, agreed through the [[@united-nations|United Nations]] in 1967, says no country can claim the Moon, planets or asteroids as its own [[territory|territory]]. It doesn't say clearly whether a company can own material it digs up.

In 2015, the USA passed a law saying its citizens can own resources they collect in space. Luxembourg passed a similar law in 2017. Some other countries argue that space resources should be shared by all of humanity. The debate is still open, and so is the question of whether asteroid mining will ever be more than an exciting idea.

text: The Moon doesn't change shape. It is always a round ball, and the Sun always lights up half of it, just as it lights up half of Earth.

As the Moon travels around Earth, we see different amounts of that lit half. When the Moon is on the far side of Earth from the Sun, we see the whole lit face: a full moon, or Purnima. When it is roughly between us and the Sun, we see only the dark side: a new moon, or Amavasya. From one new moon to the next takes about 29.5 days.

quiz.prompt: On the night of Amavasya, the new moon, where is the Moon?

options.t: Hiding behind Earth
Roughly between Earth and the Sun
On the far side of the Sun

quiz.reveal: At new moon, the Moon is roughly between us and the Sun. Its sunlit half faces away from us, so we see only the dark half, and it crosses the sky in daytime, lost in the Sun's glare.

d.try: In a dark room, put a lamp on a table at one end. Hold a ball out at arm's length and slowly turn on the spot, keeping your eyes on the ball. Watch the lit part of the ball grow from a thin crescent to full and shrink again. You are Earth, the ball is the Moon and the lamp is the Sun.
myth: The Moon's phases are caused by Earth's shadow falling on it.
Phases happen because we see different amounts of the Moon's sunlit half as it circles us. Earth's shadow only reaches the Moon during a lunar eclipse, which happens a few times at most each year.

sec.t:
After the new moon, a thin crescent appears in the west just after sunset. Each evening it grows fatter. This is the waxing Moon, called *Shukla paksha*, the bright fortnight, in [[@indian-calendars|Indian calendars]]. After about a week it is half lit, a shape [[astronomer|astronomers]] confusingly call a first quarter, because the Moon is a quarter of the way through its cycle. This is the best time to look at it through [[@stargazing|binoculars]]. Sunlight strikes the Moon from the side, so [[crater|craters]] and mountains near the edge of the lit part cast long shadows.

After the full moon it shrinks again, rising later and later each night. This is the waning Moon, *Krishna paksha*, the dark fortnight. Late in the cycle, you are more likely to spot it in the morning sky than the evening.

sec.h: The old moon in the new moon's arms

sec.t:
People have tracked the Moon for thousands of years, because its phases make an easy clock in the sky. The word "month" comes from "moon".

Many Indian [[@calendars|calendars]] are lunar or partly lunar. Diwali falls on an Amavasya in October or November, which is why so many [[@diwali-lights|lamps are lit]] on such a dark night. Holi falls on the Purnima of Phalgun. The Islamic calendar follows the Moon completely, so Eid begins when the new crescent is sighted, and it moves earlier by about 11 days each year. In the USA and Europe, the date of Easter is set by the first full moon of spring.

The Moon spins once on its [[axis|axis]] in exactly the time it takes to go around Earth. So it always keeps the same face towards us. Nobody saw the [[@moon-far-side|other side]] until the Soviet spacecraft Luna 3 photographed it in 1959. In 2019, China's Chang'e 4 became the first spacecraft to land there.

The far side is not permanently dark. It gets sunlight too. During a new moon, when our side is dark, the far side is in full daylight.
The Moon's [[gravity|gravity]] also tugs on Earth's oceans. [[@moon-tides-life|The biggest tides]] come at full moon and new moon, when the Sun and Moon pull along the same line.

text: Jupiter is the biggest planet in our [[solar-system|solar system]], about 318 times heavier than Earth. It is normally more than 590 million km away, so it looks like a bright star. Bring it much closer and its [[gravity|gravity]] would start to take charge.

At the Moon's distance, Jupiter would look about 40 times wider than the full Moon. Its pull would raise ocean tides thousands of times stronger than today's. It would also stretch the solid ground itself, heating Earth's insides, setting off earthquakes and possibly waking volcanoes. Earth's [[orbit|orbit]] around the Sun would change too. In the end, Earth might become a moon of Jupiter.

st.prompt: If Jupiter replaced our Moon at the same distance, what would happen to Earth's ocean tides?

options.t: They would be thousands of times stronger
They would stop completely
They would stay about the same

st.reveal: Tides depend on how massive and how close the pulling body is. Jupiter is about 26,000 times heavier than the Moon, so at the same distance, its tidal pull would be about that many times stronger. Coasts would be flooded and drained by enormous surges.

d.try: Feel how distance changes a pull. Hold a strong fridge magnet near a paperclip and slowly bring it closer, noting the distance where the clip jumps. Gravity works in a similar way: halve the distance and the pull gets four times stronger.
myth: Jupiter could come crashing towards Earth one day.

Planets' paths around the Sun are steady over billions of years. Computer models show Jupiter will stay roughly where it is for as long as the Sun shines normally. This "what if" is for exploring physics, not a real danger.

sec.t:
[[@jupiter-giant|Jupiter]] is about 1,40,000 km wide, 11 times wider than Earth. You could line up 11 Earths across its face. Its famous Great Red Spot is a storm wider than our whole planet.

If it hung where our Moon is, it would stretch about a ninth of the way from one horizon to the other. Its colourful stripes of cloud and swirling storms would be clear to the naked eye. On "Jupiter-lit" nights, its reflected sunlight would be bright enough to read a book by.

Tides don't only move water. They also stretch rock. Earth's solid ground already rises and falls by about 30 cm each day because of the Moon and Sun, though nobody notices.

With Jupiter nearby, the rock would flex much more. That bending produces heat, like a paperclip getting warm when you bend it back and forth. Over time, the extra heat and strain could trigger [[@earthquakes|earthquakes]] and volcanic eruptions.

We know this happens, because it is happening right now to Io. Io orbits Jupiter at about the same distance as our Moon orbits us. Jupiter's tides, helped by tugs from its other moons, keep Io's insides molten. It has more than 400 active volcanoes, some shooting plumes hundreds of kilometres high.

There is a limit to how close a moon or planet can get to a giant before being pulled apart. Scientists call it the Roche limit. For Earth near Jupiter, it would be roughly 1,00,000 km from Jupiter's centre, a little over a quarter of the Moon's distance from us.

Inside that line, Jupiter's tides would pull harder on Earth's near side than gravity holds Earth together. Our planet would be stretched and broken into a ring of rubble, like a far bigger version of Saturn's rings.

Jupiter is wrapped in a huge magnetic field that traps deadly [[radiation|radiation]]. At the Moon's distance, Earth would be inside it. Our own magnetic field would help, but astronauts and satellites would be in trouble. Earth's sky would also glow with powerful [[@aurora|auroras]], the northern and southern lights.

In real life, Jupiter stays far away. Some scientists think its gravity helps Earth by catching or flinging away [[comet|comets]] that might otherwise hit us. In 1994, the world watched comet Shoemaker-Levy 9 smash into Jupiter in more than 20 pieces.

Other scientists point out that Jupiter can also nudge [[asteroid|asteroids]] towards the inner planets. Its real role is still debated. Our own little Moon matters too, steadying Earth's tilt and seasons, and life would look very different [[@what-if-no-moon|without the Moon]].

text: The fastest animal on Earth is the [[@sky-peregrine|peregrine falcon]]. It flies high, spots a pigeon or duck below, folds its wings and dives. This dive is called a stoop. Peregrines have been measured at well over 320 km/h, faster than a car on any highway. That is close to 90 metres every second, fast enough to cross a cricket ground in under two seconds.

On land, the record goes to the cheetah, which can reach about 100 km/h, but only for a short sprint of a few hundred metres. In India, the [[@wild-blackbuck|blackbuck]] antelope can run at around 80 km/h. The [[@body-speed-limit|fastest humans]] reach about 45 km/h for a few seconds. To see how all these numbers are worked out, read about [[@speed-distance|speed and distance]].

quiz.reveal: The peregrine climbs high, folds its wings close to its body and drops. Gravity does most of the work, and its smooth, pointed shape cuts air resistance. In level flight it is fast, but nowhere near its diving speed.

d.try: Measure your own top speed. With a friend and a stopwatch, mark out 20 m in a park or playground. Run it as fast as you can while your friend times you. Divide 20 by your time in seconds, then multiply by 3.6 to get your speed in km/h.
myth: The cheetah is the fastest animal in the world.
The cheetah is the fastest land animal over a short sprint. The peregrine falcon, diving through the air, is more than three times faster.

cheetah, about 100 km/h in short sprints

sec.t:
Peregrines live on every continent except Antarctica. Like [[@bald-eagle|bald eagles]], they nearly vanished from much of North America in the 1960s because of the [[pesticide|pesticide]] DDT, and came back after it was banned.

Some now [[@urban-wildlife|live in cities]]. Tall buildings are a lot like cliffs, and cities are full of pigeons. [[@new-york|New York]] has around 30 nesting pairs on [[@skyscrapers|skyscrapers]] and bridges. In India, a resident form called the shaheen falcon nests on cliffs, and other peregrines arrive from the north each winter. Some cities put nest boxes and webcams on tall buildings, so that people can watch the chicks grow.

sec.h: Why speed is hard to measure
sec.t:
Measuring a wild animal's top speed is tricky. Animals rarely run flat out in front of a scientist with a stopwatch. Many older records came from people chasing animals in cars, or simply guessing by eye, so they can be too high or too low.

Today scientists use radar guns, very fast cameras and collars with GPS. In 2013, researchers put GPS collars on wild cheetahs in Botswana and recorded hundreds of hunting runs. The fastest was about 93 km/h, a little lower than the figure often quoted. The study showed that a cheetah's real skill is how quickly it can speed up, brake and turn. A falcon's dive is easier to measure, because scientists can film a trained bird diving from a known height.

The [[@cheetah-return|cheetah]] is a sprinter. Its long tail works like a rudder in sharp turns. It accelerates quickly but tires within a minute and must rest before it can eat. India brought cheetahs from Africa to Kuno National Park in [[@madhya-pradesh|Madhya Pradesh]] in 2022.

Over long distances, the pronghorn of North America is the champion. It can keep up a fast pace for many kilometres. In the sea, the sailfish is often called the fastest fish at around 110 km/h. Newer studies of its muscles suggest that number is far too high. Measured by body size, a tiny mite from California may beat them all: it runs over 300 times its own body length every second.

text: A lawyer is someone trained in the law who helps people understand their rights and solve legal problems. Lawyers give advice, write documents like contracts and wills, and speak for their clients in court. In India, a lawyer who argues cases in court is called an advocate.

Some lawyers defend people accused of crimes. Others help families with property, companies with deals or citizens who think the government has treated them unfairly. Whatever the case, a lawyer's job is to explain the law clearly and to stand up for their client within the rules.

A white coat, like a doctor
A curly white wig

st.reveal: Indian advocates wear a black coat and white bands at the neck, with a black gown in higher courts. The style comes from British courts. Indian lawyers don't wear the wigs still seen in some British courtrooms.

sec.t:
Much of a lawyer's day is spent reading. Laws can be long and tricky, and judges' earlier decisions shape how they apply. A lawyer has to find the rules that fit a client's problem.

Writing comes next. Lawyers draft contracts, letters and the papers that start or answer a court case. A single word can change what a contract means, so they write carefully. Only some cases reach a courtroom. There, a lawyer presents evidence, questions witnesses and argues before a [[@courts-judges|judge]]. In some American trials, a [[@jury|jury]] of ordinary citizens decides the facts.

[[@gandhi|Mahatma Gandhi]] trained as a barrister in London and went to South Africa in 1893 to work on a legal case. There he saw how Indians were treated and began his fight for equal rights. Back in India, lawyers such as Jawaharlal Nehru, Sardar Patel and B.R. Ambedkar led the independence movement and helped write the Constitution.

In the United States, [[@abraham-lincoln|Abraham Lincoln]] taught himself law by reading borrowed books and became a well-known lawyer in Illinois before he became president. Many American presidents and judges started as lawyers.

For a long time, women weren't allowed to work as lawyers. Cornelia Sorabji, who grew up in Pune, became the first woman to study law at Oxford University, starting in 1889. Back in India she worked for years to help women whose property rights were ignored. In 1924, after the rules changed, she became one of the first women allowed to practise as a lawyer in India.

Today women make up a growing share of lawyers in India and the US, and several have served as judges in the [[@supreme-courts|Supreme Court]] of each country.

In India, students can study a five-year law course after Class 12, often after taking an entrance test such as CLAT, or a three-year LLB after college. They then enrol with a State Bar Council and pass the All India Bar Examination.

In the United States, students first finish a college degree, then spend three years at law school and pass a bar exam in the state where they want to work. Good lawyers read a lot, write clearly and can see a problem from both sides. That's why debate clubs and mock trials, where students act out a pretend court case, are a popular start. Lawyers also need patience. A big case can take years. In India millions of cases are waiting to be heard at any time, which is one reason people keep arguing about how [[@laws-made|laws are made]] and how courts could work faster.

text: Most people around the world get a personal name chosen by their family, and many also carry a family name, or surname, passed down from parents. But the rules for how names are built, and in what order they go, are very different from place to place.

In the USA and much of Europe, the personal name usually comes first and the family name last. In China, Japan, Korea and Hungary it's the other way round. Many Spanish speakers carry two surnames. Icelanders name children after a parent, and many people in Myanmar or Indonesia have no family name at all. In India, all of these patterns, and a few more, can be found within one country.

st.prompt: In Iceland, a girl named Sigrid has a father called Jón. What is her last name most likely to be?

The same family surname as her grandfather
Jónsson

st.reveal: Most Icelanders take a last name meaning "son of" or "daughter of" a parent. Sigrid is Jón's daughter, so she is Sigrid Jónsdóttir. Her brother would be Jónsson. Nobody in the family needs to share a last name.

d.try: Make a family name tree. Ask parents and grandparents how they got their first names, what their surnames mean, and whether anyone's name changed when they married or moved. Draw each person with a short note about their name and see what patterns you find.
myth: Everyone in the world has a first name and a family surname.

Many people don't. Lots of people in Myanmar and Indonesia have no family name, many in Tamil Nadu use a parent's name as an initial instead, and Icelanders usually take a parent's first name. Forms with "first name" and "last name" boxes can puzzle people from all of these places.

sec.t:
In China, the family name comes before the personal name. A tiny number of family names are shared by huge numbers of people. Wang and Li are each carried by around 100 million people. In South Korea, about one person in five is a Kim.

In Japan, Korea and Hungary too, the family name comes first. When people from these countries move abroad, some switch the order to fit in, and others keep it. Since 2020 the Japanese government has asked for Japanese names in English to be written family name first.

India has many naming traditions side by side. In parts of north and west India, surnames often come from a family's old trade, village or community. Patel once meant a village headman, and Gandhi, in Gujarati, a seller of groceries and perfumes.

In Tamil Nadu, many people have no family surname. They write a parent's name as an initial before their own. In Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh, initials can stand for a home village and a father's name. The writer R.K. Narayan's initials stood for Rasipuram, a town, and Krishnaswami, his father's name. Since 1699, when [[@sikh-gurus|Guru Gobind Singh]], the tenth Sikh Guru, founded the Khalsa, many Sikh men have used the name Singh and many Sikh women Kaur. It was a way of setting aside caste names and treating everyone as equals.

Among the Akan people of Ghana, many children get a name for the day they were born. A boy born on Friday may be Kofi. A girl born on Saturday may be Ama. Many Hindu families hold a naming ceremony, the namkaran, within a few weeks of birth, and some choose a first letter based on the stars at the baby's birth.

Names also change during life. Some people take a new name at marriage, others when they join a religious order. Some simply pick a name they like better. In Iceland, a naming committee must approve any new first name that hasn't been used before. Naming customs can be a puzzle for the people who design forms and run each country's [[@census|census]]. A box marked "surname" doesn't work for someone who has never had one.

text: About 8.2 billion people live on Earth, according to [[@united-nations|United Nations]] estimates for 2024. In the Indian system, that is about 820 crore. The world passed 8 billion in November 2022.

For most of human history, the population grew very slowly. It reached 1 billion only around 1800. Then better food supplies, clean water, [[@vaccines|vaccines]] and medicines meant far more babies survived and people lived longer. The population shot up, reaching 7 billion by 2011. Now growth is slowing, as families in most countries have fewer children than their grandparents did.

It will keep doubling every 50 years

st.reveal: UN experts expect the world's population to peak at about 10.3 billion in the mid-2080s, then slowly decline, because families in most countries are having fewer children.

d.try: Estimate how many people live on your street or in your building. Count the homes, ask an adult roughly how many people live in a typical one, and multiply. Then compare with your town's population and work out how many streets like yours it would take.
myth: The world's population will keep growing forever.

Growth is already slowing. In many countries, families now have fewer than two children on average, and UN projections suggest the world's population will peak later this century and then gradually decline.

sec.t:
When people began [[@farming-began|farming]] about 10,000 years ago, there may have been only a few million humans in the whole world. Farming produced more food, so populations grew, but disease, [[famine|famine]] and war kept numbers down for thousands of years.

After 1800, things changed fast. The world went from 1 billion people to 2 billion by about 1927, and to 4 billion by 1974. Every billion now arrived in about 12 to 13 years. The [[@green-revolution|Green Revolution]] of the 1960s helped India and other countries grow far more food from the same fields.

In 2023, the UN estimated that India had overtaken [[@china-today|China]] as the world's most populous country. India now has about 1.45 billion people, or 145 crore, and China a little over 1.4 billion. The United States comes third, with about 34 crore. One in every six people on Earth lives in India.

Big numbers are hard to picture. If you counted one number every second, day and night, it would take you more than 250 years to count to 8 billion. You can explore numbers like this in [[@big-numbers|big numbers]].

All 8 billion people standing shoulder to shoulder, about four to a square metre, would fit in about 2,000 square kilometres, about one and a half times the area of [[@delhi|Delhi]]. The real challenge is not space but sharing food, water, energy and land fairly while protecting nature.

People live very unevenly. Bangladesh packs more than 17 crore people into an area smaller than the state of Andhra Pradesh, while huge parts of Canada, Australia and Russia are almost empty. More than half the world's people now live in [[@cities-grow|cities]].

Population growth is uneven across India too. Kerala and Tamil Nadu had small families early, while states such as Bihar and Uttar Pradesh still have more children per family. That is one reason why India's census numbers matter so much for planning schools, hospitals and seats in Parliament.

Families are getting smaller almost everywhere. Today the world average is about 2.3 children per woman, and in India it has fallen to about two. UN experts expect the world population to peak at about 10.3 billion in the mid-2080s and then slowly decline. Some countries, like Japan, Italy and [[@seoul|South Korea]], are already shrinking, which brings its own challenges, such as fewer young workers to care for a growing number of older people.

text: Building a big highway costs crores of rupees for every kilometre, and keeping it smooth costs more each year. A toll is a fee that drivers pay to help cover that cost.
The idea is simple: the people who use the road most pay for it most. Roads without tolls, like the street outside your home, are paid for out of [[@taxes|taxes]], shared by everyone.

quiz.prompt: Why do trucks usually pay a higher toll than cars?

news.h: New highways will get toll plazas where cars pay without stopping
news.t: On 6 November 2026, the National Highways Authority of India issued a standard design for toll plazas on four-lane and wider national highways. It sets common rules for plaza layout, lanes, lighting and signs, so every new highway can use barrier-free tolling, called Multi-Lane Free Flow. A FASTag reader and number-plate cameras on an overhead frame collect the toll while cars keep moving. The first such plaza opened at Choryasi in Gujarat on 1 May 2026, and the first six handled about 1.1 crore vehicles in three months. This entry explains why highways charge tolls at all.

d.try: On your next highway trip, look for the board at the toll plaza that lists charges. Compare the price for a car, a bus and a truck. Then guess how much heavier each one is.
myth: Once a toll road is paid for, the toll always stops.
Some tolls end when the building cost is paid back, but many continue to pay for repairs, lighting, ambulances and future widening. The rules differ from road to road and country to country.
facts: a fee paid to use a road, bridge or tunnel
the National Highways Authority of India (NHAI)
Multi-Lane Free Flow, first at Choryasi, Gujarat, 2026

sec.t:
Think of a city's free footpath and its metro. Everyone can walk on the footpath for free. But the metro is faster, cost far more to build, and needs staff to run it, so riders buy a ticket. A highway is like the metro, and the toll is its ticket.

There are two main ways a toll road gets built. Sometimes the government builds it with tax money and charges a toll to win some of it back. Often, a private company builds it and is allowed to collect tolls for a set number of years, perhaps 15 or 30, to earn its money back. After that, the road returns to the government.

[[@roads-built|Building a road]] means buying land, laying layers of stone and asphalt, and putting up [[@bridges|bridges]], lights and signs. After that come repairs, cranes to clear broken-down vehicles, ambulances and patrol vans. Tolls help pay for all of it.

The price depends on the vehicle and the distance. In India, the rates are set by the National Highways Fee Rules of 2008. Cars pay the least among four-wheelers, buses and trucks pay more, and the biggest trucks pay the most, because heavy vehicles wear out a road much faster. Rates are revised every year on 1 April, partly to keep up with [[@inflation|inflation]].

{{story:roads-built}}

Tolls go back thousands of years. The Arthashastra, an ancient Indian book on running a kingdom, describes an officer in charge of tolls collected at city gates. The [[@roman-roads|Romans]] charged fees at some bridges, and [[medieval|medieval]] towns in Europe collected tolls to fix their roads.

In 1663, England passed a law allowing tolls on part of a main road north of London. Over the next 200 years, it built thousands of turnpikes, roads blocked by a pole that was turned aside once you paid. That is where the barrier at a toll plaza comes from.

India set up the National Highways Authority of India by law in 1988, and it began work in 1995. In the early 2000s, it built the Golden Quadrilateral, about 5,800 km of highway joining Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai and Kolkata. Many new highways since then have been paid for partly by tolls.

Toll roads have grown fast in India. In 2021-22, national highways had 733 toll plazas. By 2025-26, there were 1,209. Rajasthan had the most, 172, followed by Uttar Pradesh with 141.

For years, every vehicle stopped at a booth, and drivers paid in cash. At busy plazas, long queues wasted time and fuel. So India brought in [[@fastag-tolls|FASTag]], a sticker on the windscreen with a tiny chip. A reader at the plaza talks to it using [[@radio-waves|radio waves]] and takes the money from a linked account, a bit like a [[@upi-payments|UPI payment]]. FASTag became compulsory on national highways in February 2021.

Newer plazas go further, with no barrier at all. A [[sensor|sensor]] on a metal frame above the road, called a gantry, reads the tag while cameras photograph the number plate, much like [[@how-traffic-cameras|traffic cameras]]. The first of these opened at Choryasi in Gujarat on 1 May 2026. If a payment fails, the owner gets an e-notice and has 72 hours to pay before the toll is doubled.

{{story:fastag-tolls}}

**₹70,278 crore.** The toll collected on national highways in 2025-26. In 2021-22, it was about ₹33,929 crore, so it has roughly doubled in four years.

**98%.** The share of highway tolls paid by FASTag. Cash at the booth has almost vanished.

**11.86 crore.** The number of FASTags issued by early 2026. That is roughly one tag for every 12 people in India.

**₹15.** What each crossing costs with the ₹3,000 annual pass for private cars, which covers 200 crossings. Without the pass, a single crossing can cost several times more.

**1.1 crore.** The vehicles that passed through India's first six barrier-free plazas in their first three months, without stopping.

Supporters say tolls are fair because the people who use a road pay for it, not every taxpayer. Toll money also lets roads be built faster, because companies can borrow against future tolls instead of waiting for the [[@budget-government|government's budget]].

Critics say drivers already pay road tax when they buy a vehicle, and tax on every litre of fuel, so tolls can feel like paying twice. They also complain when tolls continue on roads that are full of potholes, or when plazas sit close together. Indian rules say that on roads built with public money, the toll drops to 40% once the building cost has been recovered. Transport groups point out that trucks pay the most, and those costs can show up in the price of things the trucks carry.

**"Tolls only pay for building the road."** They also pay for repairs, lighting, cranes, ambulances and patrols, which go on for as long as the road is open.

**"Everyone pays at a toll plaza."** On national highways, motorbikes and scooters do not pay tolls. Ambulances and fire engines are also let through free.

**"No barrier means no toll."** At barrier-free plazas the cameras still see every vehicle. Drivers who do not pay get a notice, and the amount doubles if they ignore it.

For a family road trip, tolls are part of the cost, along with fuel and food. Keeping the FASTag topped up saves time at plazas. A family that drives the same highway often may save money with an annual pass.

Tolls also touch you when you are not travelling. Trucks carry vegetables, milk, medicines and school books across India, and part of what they pay in tolls ends up in what those things cost. Smooth surfaces, good lights, clear signs and ambulances on call also matter for [[@road-safety|road safety]]. Good roads help the whole [[economy|economy]], because goods and people move faster.

text: A trade deficit is when a country buys more from other countries than it sells to them. What a country sells abroad are its [[export|exports]]. What it buys are its [[import|imports]]. If imports are bigger, the difference is the trade deficit.
India usually has a trade deficit in goods, mainly because it buys a lot of oil, gold and electronics. But it sells more services, like software, than it buys, which shrinks the overall gap.

news.h: India's exports hit a record, but its goods trade gap is the widest in a year
news.t: On 13 November 2026, the commerce ministry said India sold goods worth 49.47 billion dollars abroad in October, the highest for any month in its history. But imports jumped to 89.35 billion dollars, as gold imports more than tripled before Diwali and oil cost much more, so the goods trade deficit reached 39.88 billion dollars, the biggest in a year. India also earned a surplus of about 19.8 billion dollars from services like software, which cut the overall gap to about 20 billion dollars. This entry explains what a trade deficit is and when it matters.

d.try: Keep a "family trade book" for a week. On one side, write money that comes into your home, like salaries. On the other, write money that goes out. Is there a surplus or a deficit? Then think. Did the family buy something useful, like a bicycle, that will help later? Countries ask the same question about their deficits.
myth: A trade deficit means a country is losing money and getting poorer.
A deficit only means a country is buying more than it sells. If it buys machines and materials that help it grow, it can get richer. Many strong economies run deficits for years.
facts: when a country buys more from abroad than it sells
when it sells more than it buys
what a country sells abroad; imports: what it buys
services such as software and IT, where it sells more than it buys
39.88 billion dollars, the highest in a year
the fiscal deficit, which is about the government's own budget

sec.t:
Trade is counted month by month. Officials add up the value of everything that leaves the country to be sold, and everything that arrives. Because much of world trade is priced in dollars, India's figures are usually given in dollars too.

Exports minus imports gives the trade balance:

- If exports are bigger, it is a **trade surplus**.
- If imports are bigger, it is a **trade deficit**.

There are two kinds of trade. **Goods** are things you can drop on your foot, like oil, phones, rice and cars. **Services** are things people do, like writing software, running call centres, teaching online or welcoming tourists. India runs a deficit in goods and a surplus in services.

To pay for extra imports, a country needs foreign money, or foreign [[currency|currency]]. It can get dollars from foreign companies investing, from Indians abroad sending money home, or from its own savings, called foreign exchange reserves. If a deficit grows very large for a long time, the [[@money-worth|rupee]] can weaken, making imports even dearer.

Think of a family that runs a small tiffin service. It earns money selling lunches, and spends money buying vegetables, a new stove and school books. If it spends more than it earns, that is a deficit. Whether that is a problem depends on what it bought. A new stove that helps it cook more lunches may pay for itself. Spending savings on things that do not help later is riskier.

Hundreds of years ago, many European rulers believed exports were good and imports were bad. They wanted to pile up gold by selling more than they bought. This idea was called mercantilism.

In 1776, the Scottish thinker Adam Smith argued that both sides gain from trade, because each country can focus on what it does best. Most economists since then say a deficit is not good or bad on its own. It depends on why it happens and how it is paid for.

India learned this the hard way in 1991. It had borrowed heavily and had so little foreign money left that it could pay for only about three weeks of imports. India had to pledge its gold to get loans, and then opened its [[economy|economy]] with big reforms.

{{story:trade-world}}

India imports most of its crude oil, as the story of [[@india-oil|where India gets its oil]] explains. It also buys large amounts of electronics, machinery, coal and gold. Its biggest goods exports include engineering goods, refined petrol and diesel, medicines, gems and jewellery, and rice.

In October 2026, India's goods exports reached 49.47 billion dollars, the highest for any month ever. But imports rose even faster, to 89.35 billion dollars. Gold imports more than tripled to 5.51 billion dollars as families bought before Diwali, and oil imports cost much more after a crisis in West Asia. So the goods trade deficit was 39.88 billion dollars, the largest in a year.

Services saved the day. India sold 40.51 billion dollars of services and bought 20.72 billion dollars, a surplus of almost 20 billion dollars. Counting goods and services together, India's exports were a record 89.99 billion dollars, and the overall gap was about 20 billion dollars.

- **49.47 billion dollars**: India's goods exports in October 2026, a monthly record.
- **39.88 billion dollars**: the goods trade deficit that month, the biggest in a year.
- **5.51 billion dollars**: gold imports in October 2026, more than triple the month before.
- **About 20 billion dollars**: India's services surplus that month, which roughly halved the overall gap.
- **About 3 weeks**: how many weeks of imports India's foreign money could pay for during the 1991 crisis.

Some say India should cut its trade deficit by making more at home, such as electronics and solar panels, and by putting higher taxes called [[@tariffs|tariffs]] on some imports. Others say [[tariff|tariffs]] make goods dearer for families and factories, and that India should focus on selling more abroad instead.

Gold is another debate. India mines very little [[@gold-where|gold]] of its own. Indians love gold as savings and for weddings, but importing so much widens the deficit. The government has tried gold bonds and other schemes so people can save in gold without bringing in as much metal. Abroad, some leaders, especially in the USA, see a deficit with another country as unfair. Many economists disagree.

**"A trade deficit means the country is poor."** The USA has run the world's biggest deficit for decades.

**"Trade deficit and fiscal deficit are the same."** The fiscal deficit is when the government spends more than it collects in taxes. The trade deficit is about the whole country's buying and selling with the world.

**"Only goods count."** Services, like India's software exports, count too, and they are one of India's great strengths.

The trade balance affects the value of the rupee. When the deficit is large, the rupee can weaken, which makes imported things like phones, laptops and petrol dearer, and makes studying or travelling abroad cost more. A strong export sector creates jobs in factories, farms and offices across India.

So the next time your family buys gold for a festival or a new phone, remember you are part of India's trade story. Learning [[@trade-world|why countries trade]] and [[@india-economy|how big India's economy is]] helps make sense of that monthly number.

text: "South Indian cinema" usually means films in four languages: Telugu, Tamil, [[@malayalam|Malayalam]] and Kannada. Each has its own industry, based mainly in Hyderabad, [[@chennai|Chennai]], [[@kochi|Kochi]] and Bengaluru. Together they make hundreds of films every year, and their fans are some of the most devoted anywhere.

In the last decade, these films have also crossed borders. Dubbed versions of hits such as *Baahubali*, *KGF* and *RRR* filled cinemas across north India and abroad. In 2023 the song "Naatu Naatu" from the Telugu film *RRR* won the Oscar for Best Original Song, the first for a song from an Indian film.

It is several separate industries working in different languages, each with its own stars, studios and audiences. A Malayalam film and a Telugu film can be as different as a Spanish film and a French one.

sec.t:
Telugu films are known for grand action, big sets and huge dance numbers. Tamil cinema mixes mass entertainers with sharp, small films about everyday life. Malayalam cinema, from Kerala, is often praised for realistic stories made on small budgets. Kannada cinema grew fast after the *KGF* films became national hits.

Each industry has a nickname built on [[@hollywood|Hollywood]]. Tollywood is Telugu, Kollywood comes from Kodambakkam in Chennai, Mollywood is Malayalam, and Sandalwood is Kannada, after the sandalwood trees of Karnataka.

In many southern states, a film star can be treated almost like a hero from legend. Fan clubs organise celebrations, decorate cinemas and put up cutouts several storeys high. On a big release day, some cinemas open at dawn.

That fame has carried some stars into politics. M. G. Ramachandran, a Tamil film hero, became Chief Minister of Tamil Nadu in 1977. N. T. Rama Rao, who often played gods in Telugu films, became Chief Minister of Andhra Pradesh in 1983. J. Jayalalithaa, a well-known actress, later led Tamil Nadu several times.

sec.h: Why the whole country watches now
sec.t:
For years, Hindi-speaking audiences mostly saw South Indian films as dubbed versions on TV. Those dubbed films gathered loyal fans in villages and towns of the north. When big-budget Telugu and Kannada films were released in Hindi in cinemas, a ready audience was waiting. [[@dubbing-subtitles|Dubbing]] did much of the work.

Streaming services helped too. Viewers anywhere could watch Malayalam thrillers or Tamil dramas with subtitles at home. Some film writers also say South Indian films kept faith with grand, emotional stories at a time when many Hindi films were aiming at city audiences.

Southern films have long had fans outside India. Tamil films are popular in [[@sri-lanka|Sri Lanka]], Malaysia and Singapore, where many Tamil speakers live. A 1995 Tamil film, *Muthu*, starring [[@rajinikanth|Rajinikanth]], became a surprise hit in Japan.

Telugu and Tamil films now open on the same day in the USA, the UK, the Gulf and Australia, often with special early shows for fans. Some of those fans have never been to India, but they know every word of the songs.

text: Running shoes help in two big ways. They protect your feet from the ground, and the best racing shoes give back some of the energy you put into each step.

Every time a runner's foot lands, it pushes down with a force of about two to three times their body weight. Older shoes mostly soaked up that bump. Since 2017, a new kind of racing shoe, often called a "super shoe", has shaken up the sport. It uses thick, light, very bouncy foam and a stiff plate inside the sole. Together, they work a bit like a spring, returning energy with each stride. At the top level, that has helped knock minutes off marathon records.

st.reveal: Super shoes use a very springy, light foam that gives back most of the energy squashed into it. A stiff plate, often made of carbon fibre, helps the foot roll forward and keeps the foam working well.

myth: Super shoes do the running for you, so anyone wearing them becomes an elite athlete.
They save a few percent of energy, which matters a lot at the very top, where races are won by seconds. But they can't replace years of training. A beginner in super shoes is still a beginner.
facts: Energy saved by early super shoes

sec.t:
In 1960, the Ethiopian runner Abebe Bikila lined up for the Olympic marathon in Rome. His shoes didn't fit well, so he ran barefoot over the city's stone streets. He won, and set a world best of 2:15:16.

Four years later, in Tokyo, he won again, this time wearing shoes. He was the first person to win the Olympic marathon twice in a row. His story shows that great runners come first. Shoes only help a body that is already trained.

In 1971, the American coach Bill Bowerman wanted a sole that gripped well but stayed light. At breakfast, he looked at his wife's waffle iron and poured rubber into it. The bumpy "waffle sole" became one of the first famous products of Nike, the company he co-founded.

For decades, most running shoes used a foam called EVA, the same family of material found in yoga mats and flip-flops. It cushions well, but it gets squashed flat over time and returns only part of the energy pressed into it.

In 2017, Nike launched a racing shoe with a new foam, made from a [[@plastic-made|plastic]] called PEBA. It is lighter and much bouncier. Inside the sole sat a curved plate of carbon fibre, the same strong material used in racing bikes.

A lab study tested the prototype on top runners. On average, they used about 4% less energy at the same speed. That sounds small. For a marathon runner, though, 4% can mean several minutes.

Other companies soon made their own versions. Track spikes got the same treatment, and records in races from 5,000 m to the marathon began to fall.

{{story:springs}}

When your foot lands, the foam squashes, like pressing on a [[@springs|spring]]. Good foam springs back fast and pushes your foot up and forward. The stiff plate stops your toes bending too much and helps the foot roll forward like a rocking chair.

The rubber underneath matters too. Its pattern creates [[@friction|friction]] with the road, so your push sends you forward instead of slipping.

By 2020, some people worried that shoes, not athletes, were winning races. World Athletics, which runs the sport, made new rules. Road racing shoes can have a sole no thicker than 40 mm. Spikes for track races have their own lower limits. Any shoe used in a big race must be available for anyone to buy.

In 2019, Kenya's Eliud Kipchoge ran a marathon in 1:59:40 in Vienna, but it didn't count as a record. He had rotating teams of pacers and a car showing the line to follow.

Then, at the London Marathon on 26 April 2026, Kenya's Sabastian Sawe ran 1:59:30 in a normal race. He became the first person to break two hours in a record-eligible marathon. Shoes played a part, but so did training, [[nutrition|nutrition]] and smart pacing.

Shoes are only one piece of the speed puzzle. Starting blocks, arm swings and leg power matter as much to the fastest people alive, as the science of [[@sport-science-sprinting|sprinting]] shows.

text: Your heart is a muscle about the size of your fist. It [[@heart-beat|beats]] around 1 lakh times a day, pushing [[@blood|blood]] through four chambers and out to the body. It can go wrong in a few main ways. The pipes that feed it can get blocked. Its valves can leak or stick. Its electrical [[rhythm|rhythm]] can go haywire, or a baby can be born with a part shaped wrongly.

Doctors have a fix for each. Some need only a thin tube slid in through a blood vessel. Others need open-heart surgery, where the chest is opened and a machine keeps the patient alive while the heart is still. When a heart is too damaged to repair, a [[@transplants|transplant]] from a donor may be the answer. Almost none of this was possible before the 1940s.

myth: In a heart transplant or bypass, doctors usually replace the whole heart with an artificial one.

Most heart operations repair the person's own heart, such as fixing a valve or adding new pipes around blocked arteries. Transplants use a donated human heart. Fully artificial hearts exist but are rare and are mostly used for a short time while someone waits for a donor.
facts: Babies born with a heart problem

sec.t:
About 1 baby in every 100 is born with some kind of heart problem. Some are born with a heart that doesn't send enough blood to the lungs. Their skin looks bluish, so they were called "blue babies". In the early 1940s, a doctor named Helen Taussig in Baltimore thought a new connection between two blood vessels might help.

[[surgeon|Surgeon]] Alfred Blalock and his lab technician, Vivien Thomas, worked out how. Thomas, a Black man who had to give up his dream of college for lack of money, practised the operation on animals until it was reliable. In 1944, Blalock performed it on a tiny girl named Eileen Saxon, with Thomas standing behind him giving advice. She turned pink on the table. For many years Thomas got little credit, but Johns Hopkins later gave him an honorary doctorate.

The most common heart trouble in adults is a blocked coronary [[artery|artery]], one of the small pipes that feed the heart muscle itself. Fatty deposits build up inside it, as hard water leaves crust inside a kettle.

One fix is a bypass. The surgeon takes a spare piece of [[vein|vein]] from the leg, or an artery from the chest wall. It is sewn around the blockage, like a new road built around a traffic jam. Many patients get three or four bypasses in one operation. A gentler fix is angioplasty, first done in Zurich in 1977. A tiny balloon is pushed up to the blockage and inflated. Often a little mesh tube called a stent is left in place to keep the artery open. The patient is usually awake throughout.

The heart has its own electrical system that tells it when to squeeze. If it slows down or skips, a pacemaker can help. This matchbox-sized device sits under the skin near the collarbone, with a wire to the heart, and sends small pulses to keep the rhythm steady.

The first implanted pacemaker went into a Swedish engineer named Arne Larsson in 1958. He needed many replacements over the years, and lived to 86, longer than both the doctor and the engineer who made his first one. In India, hospitals such as Narayana Health in [[@bengaluru|Bengaluru]] have become known for doing heart surgery at much lower cost than many other countries.

text: Your kidneys are two bean-shaped organs at the back of your belly. Their main job is to clean your [[@blood|blood]]. Blood flows into each kidney through a big [[artery|artery]], gets filtered, and flows out again cleaner.

The waste, along with any extra water and [[@salt|salt]], becomes urine. It trickles down two thin tubes into your bladder, which stores it until you go to the toilet. Kidneys also decide how much water to keep, help control blood pressure, and send out a signal that tells your bones to make more red blood cells. They are small, but they get about a fifth of all the blood your heart pumps.

Low down in the front, near the belly button
Low in the back, at the waistband

st.reveal: Your kidneys sit high at the back of your belly, one on each side of your spine. The lowest ribs give them some protection. The right one sits a little lower than the left because the liver is above it.

d.try: For a day, check the colour of your wee each time you go and compare it to a pale straw or a lemonade colour. Write down what you drank in the hours before. You will see your kidneys making more water when you drink more and saving water when you drink less.
myth: Your kidneys are low down in your lower back, near your waist.
They are higher than most people think, tucked under the back of the ribcage on either side of the spine. Pain low in the back is usually from muscles, not kidneys.

sec.t:
Each kidney contains about a million filtering units called nephrons. Each nephron starts with a tiny knot of blood vessels inside a cup. Water, salt, sugar and waste are pushed out of the blood into the cup, leaving blood cells and big [[protein|proteins]] behind.

That fluid then flows along a long, looping tube. Along the way, the kidney takes back almost everything useful, including nearly all the water and sugar. Of the 180 litres or so filtered each day, only 1 or 2 litres leave as urine. The kidney is like a person who empties their whole school bag onto the floor every few minutes, then puts back everything except the rubbish.

sec.h: A machine made from sausage skins
sec.t:
Kidneys can be damaged by illness, injury or long-lasting high blood pressure or diabetes. When both stop working, waste builds up in the blood and makes a person very ill.

In 1943, in the occupied Netherlands during the [[@world-war-two|Second World War]], a young doctor named Willem Kolff built a machine to do the kidneys' job. He used sausage casings as filters, wrapped around a drum that turned in a tub of cleaning fluid, with parts from orange juice cans and a washing machine. His first patients didn't survive, but in 1945 a woman did. Today's version is called dialysis, and millions of people around the world rely on it.

sec.h: Twin brothers and a new kidney
sec.t:
The other answer is a [[@transplants|transplant]]: a new kidney from a [[@organ-donation|donor]]. The trouble is that the body attacks tissue that isn't its own. In 1954, in Boston, a doctor named Joseph Murray found a way around this. Richard Herrick's kidneys were failing, and his identical [[@twins|twin]] Ronald offered one of his. Because identical twins have the same [[gene|genes]], Richard's body accepted it.

It was the first successful organ transplant in history. Murray later won a Nobel Prize. Ronald lived for decades more with one kidney, which shows how much spare capacity a healthy kidney has. Today, medicines that calm the [[@immune-system|immune system]] let people receive kidneys from donors who aren't twins.

text: Your liver is a large, reddish-brown organ tucked under your ribs on the right side. It works like a factory, a warehouse and a cleaning plant all in one.

Blood coming from your gut, full of everything you've just digested, goes straight to the liver first. The liver sorts it. It stores some sugar for later, packs away iron and [[vitamin|vitamins]], and builds [[protein|proteins]] your [[@blood|blood]] needs, including the ones that make it clot when you cut yourself. It also breaks down things the body doesn't want, such as old blood cells and medicines that have done their job. And it makes bile, a green-yellow liquid that helps you digest fat.

st.prompt: Surgeons remove half of a healthy person's liver. What happens next?

options.t: The remaining part grows back to nearly full size in a few months
The person must live with half a liver forever
The liver stops working until a new one is put in

st.reveal: The liver can regrow from a healthy piece. Its cells start dividing and keep going until the organ is close to its old size, usually within a few months. It doesn't grow back the same shape, but it does the same work.

src: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Liver.
American Liver Foundation, The Liver.

d.try: Make a liver jobs chart. Draw a large liver shape and write one of its jobs on a sticky note every time you read about one here, such as making bile or storing iron. See how many you can fit, then compare with your heart, which mostly does one job.
myth: The liver can regrow, so nothing can really harm it.

The liver can heal from a lot, but long-lasting damage, for example from heavy drinking of alcohol or some viruses, can leave scars. Scarred liver can't do its work, and it doesn't grow back the way healthy liver does.
facts: largest organ inside the body (the skin is larger, on the outside)
more than 500, by many doctors' counts

sec.t:
After a meal, there is more sugar in your blood than you need right away. The liver packs the extra into a starch-like store called glycogen. Hours later, when you're running around or asleep, it turns that store back into sugar to keep your brain fed.

It also holds stocks of vitamin A, vitamin D, vitamin B12 and iron. Some of these stores can last for months. This is one reason a person doesn't fall ill the day they miss a few [[@vitamins|vitamins]].

Many substances that enter the body need to be made safe before they can leave. The liver changes them, using [[enzyme|enzymes]], into forms that can go out in bile or be passed to the [[@kidneys|kidneys]] and leave in urine.

When red blood cells wear out, after about four months, the liver helps handle the yellow [[pigment|pigment]] left over. If this pigment builds up, the skin and the whites of the eyes turn yellow. This is called jaundice. Many newborn babies get mild jaundice in their first week, because their livers are still getting started. Doctors watch it, and it usually clears by itself or with a simple light treatment.

The liver's work also matters for medicines. It breaks most of them down, which is why a dose wears off after a few hours. Children's livers handle some medicines differently from adults', so doctors and pharmacists choose doses by age and weight. All that chemical work also gives off heat. Resting, the liver is one of the body's main sources of warmth.

{{story:greek-myths}}

Most organs can't replace large lost pieces. The liver can. If part of it is removed, the [[cell|cells]] that remain start to divide until the liver reaches close to its old size. This is what makes [[@transplants|living donor transplants]] possible: a healthy adult gives part of their liver to someone whose liver is failing, often a family member.

The first liver transplant was tried by [[surgeon|surgeon]] Thomas Starzl in the USA in 1963. Today, [[@hospitals|hospitals]] around the world, including many in India, do thousands of these operations every year. A good share of them use living donors.

Bile drips out of the liver all the time. Between meals it is stored in a small pouch under the liver called the gall bladder. When fatty food arrives in your gut, the gall bladder squeezes bile into the small intestine. Bile breaks fat into tiny droplets, the way washing-up liquid breaks up grease on a plate. That gives digestive enzymes more surface to work on.

Bile is also what gives poo its brown colour. The pigments from old blood cells travel out in bile and change colour on their way through the gut.

text: Thomas Jefferson was one of the Founding Fathers of the United States. He wrote most of the Declaration of Independence in 1776, which announced that the American colonies were breaking away from Britain. Later he was the third president, from 1801 to 1809.

He was a lawyer, a farmer, an architect, an inventor and a collector of books. He doubled the size of the US with the Louisiana Purchase and founded the University of Virginia. But the man who wrote that all people have a right to liberty also enslaved hundreds of people. Both facts are part of his story.

st.prompt: In 1803, Jefferson's government bought a huge area of land from France. About how much did it add to the United States?

options.t: It roughly doubled the size of the country
It added one small state
It added only the city of New Orleans

st.reveal: The Louisiana Purchase covered about 2.1 million square kilometres, stretching from the Mississippi River to the Rocky Mountains. The US paid France about 15 million dollars, which works out at less than 3 cents an acre.

sec.h: The words that started a country
sec.t:
In June 1776, the Continental Congress asked a committee to write a statement explaining why the colonies were declaring independence. The committee, which included [[@benjamin-franklin|Benjamin Franklin]] and John Adams, handed the job to Jefferson, then 33.

He wrote it in about two weeks, in rented rooms in Philadelphia. The most famous line says that "all men are created equal" and have rights to "life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness". Congress made changes, including cutting a section where Jefferson blamed the British king for the slave trade. On 4 July 1776, they approved it.

Those words became a promise that later movements would point to, from campaigners against slavery to women seeking the vote.

Jefferson designed his own home, Monticello, on a hilltop in Virginia, and kept changing it for 40 years. It had a dome, clever dumbwaiters for carrying wine between floors, and a clock that showed the day of the week. He loved gadgets, including a machine that copied his letters as he wrote them.

He owned one of the largest book collections in America. When British troops burned the Library of Congress in 1814, Jefferson sold his roughly 6,500 books to rebuild it, which is why [[@libraries|libraries]] in the US owe him a debt.

Jefferson enslaved more than 600 people over his life. They built and ran Monticello, farmed his land and served his family. He called slavery wrong and a danger to the nation, but freed only a few of the people he enslaved.

Sally Hemings was an enslaved woman at Monticello. Evidence, including a DNA study in 1998, has led most historians to conclude that Jefferson fathered her six children, four of whom survived. Monticello, now a museum, tells the stories of the enslaved families alongside his.

Jefferson's face is on the US nickel and on Mount Rushmore, and the Jefferson Memorial stands in Washington, DC. He asked that his gravestone list only three things: the Declaration of Independence, a Virginia law on religious freedom, and the University of Virginia. It doesn't mention that he was president.

Today, Americans still debate how to remember him. Many admire his ideas about freedom and [[@democracy-what|democracy]]. Many also point out that he did not live up to them. Both views are common, and historians keep studying the gap between his words and his life.

text: An idiom is a group of words that means something different from the words on their own. "Spill the beans" has nothing to do with beans. "It's a piece of cake" is not about cake. You only understand an idiom if someone has taught you, or if you have heard it enough times to guess.

Most idioms started as plain descriptions of real things: ships, horses, games, farms and kitchens. Over time people used them for other situations, and the original picture faded. Some came from famous writers. Others came from sport. Many are so old that nobody knows who said them first.
The word itself comes from the Greek *idioma*, meaning something peculiar to one place or person. That fits. Idioms are the private jokes of a language, and you have to be inside to get them.

st.prompt: The phrase "saved by the bell" really comes from which of these?

Coffins fitted with bells in case someone was buried alive
School bells ringing before a test

st.reveal: A boxer who is about to lose can be saved when the bell ends the round. The phrase appears in boxing reports from the late 1800s. The story about coffins with bells is popular but has no good evidence behind it.

myth: "Raining cats and dogs" comes from pets sliding off thatched roofs in heavy rain.
There is no evidence for this. The phrase has been in use since at least the 1600s, and word experts still don't know where it began.

hit for six, on a sticky wicket

sec.t:
Young children often take idioms literally. Tell a five-year-old that you have "butterflies in your stomach" and they may look worried. By about eight or nine, most children understand that the words are a picture. The butterflies are really that fluttery feeling of [[@fear|fear]] before a test or a match.

Adults who learn a new language find idioms among the hardest parts. You can know every word in "kick the bucket" and still have no idea that it means to die.

A playwright speaking to big crowds every night could launch a phrase across a whole country. [[@shakespeare|William Shakespeare]] is the earliest known writer of "wild-goose chase", in *Romeo and Juliet*. Back then it meant a horse race where riders had to follow the leader's twists and turns, like geese flying in a line. Today it means a pointless hunt.

He also used "break the ice" in *The Taming of the Shrew*. That one is older than him. It first described ships cutting a path through frozen water so other boats could follow. Opening a channel became a way of saying "starting the conversation".

Every language grows its own. Hindi has "naach na jaane aangan tedha": someone who can't dance blames the crooked courtyard. Another, "oont ke munh mein jeera", means a cumin seed in a camel's mouth, for a portion far too small to matter. An English speaker might say "a drop in the ocean" for the same thing.

These are hard to carry across languages. Word for word, a [[@translation|translation]] of "it's raining cats and dogs" makes no sense in Kannada or Spanish. Good translators look for a phrase that does the same job in the new language, even if the picture is completely different.

sec.h: When the story is a guess
sec.t:
Because idioms are fun, people love inventing tales about them. You may hear that "raining cats and dogs" comes from animals falling off roofs, or that "saved by the bell" comes from coffins with bells. Neither story has real evidence.

Experts who build [[@dictionaries|dictionaries]] hunt for the oldest written example of a phrase. Sometimes they find it in a play, a newspaper or a letter. Often the trail goes cold, and the honest answer is "we don't know". That hasn't stopped anyone from using the phrase. People were saying cats and dogs came down from the sky long before anyone thought to ask why.

text: Burgers and hot dogs came to the USA with German [[@ellis-island|immigrants]] in the 1800s. In Hamburg, people ate a kind of minced beef patty, and in Frankfurt and Vienna they ate long, thin sausages. Millions of Germans moved to America, bringing these foods with them.

In the busy cities of the late 1800s, working people needed quick, cheap meals they could eat standing up or on the move. Putting a beef patty or a sausage inside a bun did the trick. Fairs, [[@baseball-world-series|baseball]] games and, later, [[@fast-food-history|roadside restaurants for car drivers]] made them part of everyday American life.

d.try: Do a survey of 10 friends or family members. Ask each one to name their favourite thing to eat in a bun, such as a burger, hot dog, vada pav or something else. Draw a bar chart of the results. Then ask the oldest person you know what they ate in a bun as a child.
myth: Hamburgers are made from ham.
Hamburgers are traditionally made from minced beef. The name comes from the city of Hamburg in Germany, where people ate seasoned minced meat. The "ham" in hamburger has nothing to do with pork.

sec.t:
Nobody knows for sure. Several places in the USA claim the first hamburger. A restaurant in New Haven, Connecticut, says it served one in 1900. A man in Seymour, Wisconsin, is said to have flattened meatballs into a bun at a fair in 1885. Two brothers from Ohio say they sold one in Hamburg, New York, the same year.

In 2000, the Library of Congress recorded New Haven's claim in a project on local traditions. But the other towns still disagree, and historians say there is no real way to settle the question. The likeliest answer is that many people had the same simple idea around the same time. By the early 1900s, hamburgers were being sold at fairs across the country.

In 1921, a restaurant called White Castle opened in Wichita, Kansas. It sold small, cheap burgers made in a clean kitchen customers could see, and grew into the first burger chain.

After the [[@world-war-two|Second World War]], Americans bought [[@cars-history|cars]] in huge numbers and drove along new [[@route-66|highways]]. Roadside burger stands grew into big chains. In 1948, Richard and Maurice McDonald rebuilt their restaurant in California around a fast assembly-line kitchen. A businessman named Ray Kroc later turned McDonald's into one of the biggest restaurant companies in the world.

When McDonald's came to India in 1996, it had to change its menu. Many Hindus don't eat beef and many Muslims don't eat pork, so neither was served. Chicken, fish and vegetable patties took their place, and kitchens kept vegetarian food separate.

The McAloo Tikki, a spiced potato patty in a bun, became one of its best sellers. In a country where many people are [[@vegetarian|vegetarian]], the potato burger made sense.

India had a bun snack long before the chains arrived. Vada pav, a spiced potato fritter in a soft pav roll, is often called [[@mumbai|Mumbai]]'s burger. It is usually traced to a stall near Dadar station in the 1960s, where it fed [[textile|textile]] mill workers on the go.

It's cheap, filling and quick, the same reasons Americans took to burgers a century ago. Today, vada pav stalls sit outside almost every railway station in Mumbai, as you can read in [[@street-food|Indian street food]].

text: People have eaten with knives and spoons for thousands of years, but the table fork is a newcomer. Romans had large forks for serving and cooking, and small eating forks were used in the Byzantine Empire, the eastern half of the old Roman world. From there they reached Italy around the year 1000.

The rest of Europe took centuries to catch on. Forks were rare in England until the late 1600s and only became normal in the USA in the 1800s. Meanwhile, much of the world never needed them at all: around a fifth of people eat with [[@food-chopsticks|chopsticks]], and many more eat [[@food-eating-with-hands|with their hands]].

Everyone copied him within a year
The king made forks compulsory at court

st.reveal: Thomas Coryat brought the habit home from Italy and wrote about it in 1611. Friends teased him with the Latin nickname "Furcifer", which can mean fork-bearer but also rascal. It took England about another century to come round.

d.try: Eat one meal at home with only a spoon, and one with only a fork (with a grown-up's OK). Notice which foods get hard. Then think about which tool was invented to solve which problem. Peas, noodles and rice will tell you a lot.
myth: Catherine de' Medici brought the fork to France when she married the future French king in 1533.
This story is told everywhere, but historians have found little evidence for it. Forks spread through France slowly, over more than a century, and nobody can pin it on one person.

sec.h: Knife first, by a very long way

sec.t:
Around the year 1004, a Byzantine princess married the son of the ruler of Venice. At the wedding feast she would not touch food with her fingers. Instead, a servant cut it up and she ate using a little two-pronged golden fork.

A churchman called Peter Damian later wrote about her with disgust, calling such delicacy a sin of pride. When she died young of an illness, some writers hinted it was a punishment. Forks, at the time, looked like a silly luxury from the East.

Italians adopted forks anyway, partly because they ate so much slippery pasta. In 1608 an Englishman named Thomas Coryat walked across Europe and was amazed to see Italians using forks. He brought the habit home and described it in his travel book of 1611. His friends mocked him for it.

The early forks had two straight prongs, good for holding meat still while you cut. Food kept sliding off, though. By the 1700s, makers in Germany and France were adding a third and fourth prong and curving them slightly, until a fork could scoop as well as stab.

Forks arrived in the American colonies late, and for years many families ate with a knife and a big spoon. When forks did spread in the 1800s, Americans developed their own habit. They cut food with the knife in the right hand, put the knife down, then swap the fork into the right hand to eat. Europeans keep the fork in the left hand throughout. Etiquette writers still argue over which is proper.

Cheap [[@steel|steel]] and factory production finally put forks in every kitchen drawer. Stainless steel, invented in the early 1900s, made them shiny and rust-free.

In India, eating with the right hand remained the normal way for most meals, and still is. Spoons were used for serving and for some foods, and the British brought the full set of knives and forks into [[colonial|colonial]] clubs and hotels. Today many Indian families switch happily: fingers for rice and dal, a spoon for curd, a fork for noodles.

That choice isn't just habit. Some people swear food tastes better eaten by hand, and there is a little science behind the idea, explored in [[@food-eating-with-hands|eating with your hands]].

text: Soap is made by mixing fat or oil with an [[alkali|alkali]], a strong substance such as lye made from wood ash. When the two are heated together, they react and turn into soap. Chemists call this reaction saponification, from the Latin word for soap.

People in Mesopotamia knew how to do this more than 4,000 years ago. Clay tablets describe boiling fats with ash. For a long time, soap was used mainly for cleaning wool and cloth, and for treating skin. Washing yourself with soap every day became common only in the last couple of hundred years.

st.prompt: How does soap get greasy dirt off your hands?

options.t: One end of each soap molecule grabs oil, the other end grabs water
Soap dissolves the top layer of your skin
Soap makes dirt so heavy that it falls off

st.reveal: A soap molecule is like a tiny tadpole. Its tail clings to grease and its head clings to water. Thousands of tails surround a blob of grease, and when you rinse, the water pulls the heads, and the grease, away.

d.try: Fill a plate with water and shake ground black pepper over the surface. Dip a clean finger in, and not much happens. Now put a drop of liquid soap on your fingertip and touch the middle. Watch the pepper rush away to the edges as the soap breaks the water's surface.
myth: Soap is named after Mount Sapo near Rome, where melted animal fat ran down into the river.
This story is often repeated, but historians have found no evidence that a Mount Sapo ever existed. The Latin word sapo probably came from a Germanic word for a kind of grease or dye.
facts: fat or oil plus an alkali, such as lye

sec.t:
The oldest written soap recipes come from [[@mesopotamia|Mesopotamia]], in what is now Iraq. Clay tablets more than 4,000 years old describe mixing water, alkali and cassia oil. In [[@ancient-egypt|ancient Egypt]], a medical scroll called the Ebers Papyrus, from about 1550 BCE, describes mixing animal and vegetable oils with alkaline salts for washing and treating skin.

The Romans used soap less than you might expect. Wealthy Romans cleaned themselves by rubbing oil on their skin and scraping it off with a curved metal tool.

In the Middle Ages, soap makers in Syria, Spain and Italy made hard bars from olive oil. Aleppo soap, with olive oil and laurel oil, has been made in Syria for centuries.

In India, people often washed with natural cleansers. Reetha, or soapnut, makes a gentle lather when soaked in water. Shikakai pods were used to wash hair. In the early 1800s, Sake Dean Mahomed, a traveller from Bihar, opened a bathhouse in Brighton, England, offering "shampooing", an Indian head massage. The word stuck in English.

In 1847 a Hungarian doctor named Ignaz Semmelweis worked in a hospital in Vienna. Many mothers were dying of fever after giving birth. He made doctors wash their hands in a chlorine solution before examining patients, and deaths fell sharply.

Other doctors mocked him at first. Only later, when scientists proved that germs cause disease, did handwashing become a basic rule of [[@doctors-history|medicine]]. Today the World Health Organization calls handwashing with soap one of the simplest ways to prevent illness.

In the 1800s, factories began making soap cheaply. In 1884 Lever Brothers in England launched Sunlight soap, and soon shipped it to India and around the world.

In 1916 the Maharaja of Mysore, Krishnaraja Wadiyar IV, set up a government soap factory in [[@bengaluru|Bengaluru]] to use the region's sandalwood oil. Mysore Sandal Soap is still made there.

Modern detergents, like washing powder, work the same way as soap but are made from different chemicals. They clean better in hard water, which leaves soap scum. But a simple bar of soap still does the most important job: washing away germs with nothing more than a lather and a rinse.
